## What we asked

Week 1's playground is the network of all 303 characters in Wikipedia's
[Category:Marvel Comics superheroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Marvel_Comics_superheroes),
linked by whichever internal wiki-links their articles actually contain. This is the bootstrap
post, so we stuck to the assignment's core prompt rather than chasing a tangent:

- What do the in-degree and out-degree distributions look like, on linear and on log-log axes?
- Who gets linked to the most, who links out the most — and why are those different people?
- Draw the network. Find the islands outside the giant component.

Everything below is computed live from the frozen week-1 snapshot (`week1_nodes.tsv` /
`week1_edges.tsv`, released 2026-08-26) — every headline number is backed by an `assert` against
the network's own structure, not typed in from memory.

## Loading the network without losing the isolates

17 of the 303 characters have no link in either direction. Building the graph from the edge list
alone would silently drop them, so every node gets added before a single edge does.

```{python}
import math

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

nodes = pd.read_csv("data/week1_nodes.tsv", sep="\t", comment="#",
                     quoting=3)  # QUOTE_NONE: TSVs never quote, but blurbs may contain "quotes"
edges = pd.read_csv("data/week1_edges.tsv", sep="\t", comment="#",
                     names=["source", "target"])

G = nx.DiGraph()
G.add_nodes_from(nodes.node_id)
G.add_edges_from(edges.itertuples(index=False))

assert G.number_of_nodes() == 303, G.number_of_nodes()
assert G.number_of_edges() == 1784, G.number_of_edges()
print(f"Directed graph: {G.number_of_nodes()} nodes, {G.number_of_edges()} edges")

name_lookup = dict(zip(nodes.node_id, nodes.name))
```

## Reconciling directed vs. undirected

```{python}
G_und = G.to_undirected()  # default reciprocal=False: "connected at all, either direction"
n = G_und.number_of_nodes()
m_und = G_und.number_of_edges()
avg_k = 2 * m_und / n

assert m_und == 1434, m_und
print(f"Undirected: {m_und} edges, average degree <k> = 2m/n = {avg_k:.2f}")

mutual_pairs = sum(1 for u, v in G.edges() if G.has_edge(v, u)) // 2
assert mutual_pairs == 350, mutual_pairs
print(f"Reciprocated (mutual) pairs: {mutual_pairs}")
print(f"{G.number_of_edges()} directed edges - {mutual_pairs} mutual pairs = "
      f"{G.number_of_edges() - mutual_pairs} undirected edges")

density = m_und / (n * (n - 1) / 2)
print(f"Density: {density:.3f} — about {density:.0%} of all possible pairs are connected")
```

Each mutual pair contributes two directed edges (A→B and B→A) but only one undirected edge, so
the directed and undirected edge counts differ by exactly the number of mutual pairs. Average
in-degree and average out-degree must be equal (both are just $m/n$, since every directed edge
has exactly one tail and one head) — that symmetry is a property of *any* directed graph, not
something special about this one.

## The giant component — and the islands outside it

This is the part last week's exercise notebook never actually computed: which characters sit
outside the network's one big connected blob?

```{python}
comps = sorted(nx.connected_components(G_und), key=len, reverse=True)

sizes = [len(c) for c in comps]
assert sizes == [277, 9] + [1] * 17, sizes
assert sum(sizes) == 303

giant, island = comps[0], comps[1]
isolates = set().union(*comps[2:])

print(f"{len(comps)} connected components total")
print(f"  giant component: {len(giant)} characters ({len(giant)/n:.0%} of the network)")
print(f"  one island:      {len(island)} characters")
print(f"  isolates:        {len(isolates)} characters, each its own component")
print(f"  {len(giant)} + {len(island)} + {len(isolates)} = {len(giant) + len(island) + len(isolates)}")
```

```{python}
print("The 9-character island:")
for node_id in sorted(island, key=lambda x: name_lookup[x]):
    print(f"  {name_lookup[node_id]}")
```

That island isn't a random grab-bag — it's essentially the entire 1980s *Strikeforce: Morituri*
spin-off squad, wiki-linked tightly to each other and to almost nobody else in the mainstream
Marvel universe pages. More on this in "what surprised us" below.

## In-degree vs. out-degree distributions

Plotted against $k+1$ on every axis, since a log axis can't show zero and 17 characters have
in- or out-degree 0.

```{python}
def raw_distribution(values):
    """values: iterable of raw non-negative integers (e.g. degrees). Returns sorted {v+1: count}."""
    counts = {}
    for v in values:
        u = v + 1
        counts[u] = counts.get(u, 0) + 1
    return dict(sorted(counts.items()))

in_degrees = [d for _, d in G.in_degree()]
out_degrees = [d for _, d in G.out_degree()]

in_dist = raw_distribution(in_degrees)
out_dist = raw_distribution(out_degrees)

print(f"in-degree range: 0 to {max(in_degrees)}")
print(f"out-degree range: 0 to {max(out_degrees)}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-degree-raw
#| fig-cap: "In-degree and out-degree, linear (left) and log-log (right), plotted against k+1."

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 9))

for row, (dist, title) in enumerate([(in_dist, "In-degree"), (out_dist, "Out-degree")]):
    u_vals = list(dist.keys())
    counts = list(dist.values())

    ax_lin = axes[row, 0]
    ax_lin.bar(u_vals, counts, width=0.8, color="steelblue")
    ax_lin.set_title(f"{title} (linear)")
    ax_lin.set_xlabel("k + 1")
    ax_lin.set_ylabel("number of nodes")

    ax_log = axes[row, 1]
    ax_log.scatter(u_vals, counts, s=20, color="steelblue")
    ax_log.set_xscale("log")
    ax_log.set_yscale("log")
    ax_log.set_title(f"{title} (log-log)")
    ax_log.set_xlabel("k + 1 (log scale; the +1 keeps the isolates visible)")
    ax_log.set_ylabel("number of nodes (log scale)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
def top5(degree_view, label):
    ranked = sorted(degree_view, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:5]
    print(f"Top 5 by {label}:")
    for node_id, k in ranked:
        print(f"  {name_lookup[node_id]}: {k}")

top5(G.in_degree(), "in-degree")
print()
top5(G.out_degree(), "out-degree")
```

## Binning, per the course's exact scheme

Working in $u = k+1$: width-1 bins for $u = 1, \dots, 7$, then doubling bins with **integer**
edges — $[8,16)$, $[16,32)$, $[32,64)$, $[64,128)$ — never `np.logspace`, so every bin holds a
known, exact set of integers and none is empty by construction. Each bin's count is divided by
its width (a density per unit degree), and each bin is drawn at the geometric mean of the
*integers it covers*.

```{python}
def bin_edges(max_u):
    """Integer edges: width-1 for u=1..7 (edges 1..8), then doubling (8,16,32,...) past max_u."""
    edges = list(range(1, 9))  # 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8 -> seven width-1 bins covering u=1..7
    while edges[-1] <= max_u:
        edges.append(edges[-1] * 2)
    return edges


def binned_distribution(dist):
    """dist: {u: count}. Returns (xs, ys): bin position (geometric mean of covered integers)
    and density (count / bin width)."""
    edges = bin_edges(max(dist))
    xs, ys = [], []
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        width = hi - lo
        count = sum(c for u, c in dist.items() if lo <= u < hi)
        xs.append(np.sqrt(lo * (hi - 1)))
        ys.append(count / width)
    return xs, ys


in_bin_x, in_bin_y = binned_distribution(in_dist)
out_bin_x, out_bin_y = binned_distribution(out_dist)


def check_width1_matches_raw(dist, xs, ys, n_width1=7):
    for i in range(n_width1):
        u = i + 1
        assert abs(xs[i] - u) < 1e-9, (xs[i], u)
        assert abs(ys[i] - dist.get(u, 0)) < 1e-9, (ys[i], dist.get(u, 0))

check_width1_matches_raw(in_dist, in_bin_x, in_bin_y)
check_width1_matches_raw(out_dist, out_bin_x, out_bin_y)
print("Sanity check passed: binned values exactly match raw P(u) for every width-1 bin (u = 1..7).")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-degree-binned
#| fig-cap: "Raw vs. binned in-degree and out-degree, log-log. The binned curve sits exactly on the raw points where bins are width 1, and only smooths where the data thins."

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))

for ax, (dist, bin_x, bin_y, title) in zip(
    axes,
    [(in_dist, in_bin_x, in_bin_y, "In-degree"), (out_dist, out_bin_x, out_bin_y, "Out-degree")],
):
    ax.scatter(list(dist.keys()), list(dist.values()), s=15, color="lightgray", label="raw")
    ax.plot(bin_x, bin_y, "o-", color="crimson", label="binned")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_title(f"{title}: raw vs. binned (log-log)")
    ax.set_xlabel("k + 1")
    ax.set_ylabel("density (nodes / bin width)")
    ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

(We don't fit a power-law slope to this — never fit a slope to binned, shifted data. Reading the
shape is this week's job; the cumulative distribution that actually supports fitting arrives in
week 2.)

## Why do the in-degree and out-degree leaders differ?

The two top-5 lists above barely overlap, and that's not a coincidence — it's about *who creates*
each kind of edge. An in-link is **conferred**: some other article's editors decided this
character was worth mentioning and linking to. An out-link is **authored**: someone had to sit
down and write it into *this* page. Conferred links have no natural ceiling — every other article
in the encyclopedia is a potential source — which is exactly why Spider-Man's in-degree (106) can
run so far ahead of the pack. Authored links are bounded by one editor's patience on one article,
which is why even the most link-happy page, Betsy Braddock's, tops out at 28.

```{python}
#| label: fig-inout-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Out-degree vs. in-degree per character. The top-5 by each measure are almost entirely different people."

top_in_ids = {nid for nid, _ in sorted(G.in_degree(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:5]}
top_out_ids = {nid for nid, _ in sorted(G.out_degree(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:5]}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
xs = [G.out_degree(nid) for nid in G.nodes()]
ys = [G.in_degree(nid) for nid in G.nodes()]
ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=18, color="lightgray", zorder=1)

for nid in top_in_ids | top_out_ids:
    x, y = G.out_degree(nid), G.in_degree(nid)
    color = "#c8102e" if nid in top_in_ids else "#1f77b4"
    ax.scatter([x], [y], s=45, color=color, zorder=2)
    ax.annotate(name_lookup[nid], (x, y), fontsize=8, xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points")

ax.set_xlabel("out-degree")
ax.set_ylabel("in-degree")
ax.set_title("In-degree vs. out-degree (red = top-5 in-degree, blue = top-5 out-degree)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

None of the top-5-by-out-degree characters crack the top-5-by-in-degree list, and vice versa —
the two measures are picking out genuinely different kinds of "important."

## Drawing the network

All 303 characters, colored by which of the three populations they belong to. The giant
component gets a force-directed layout; the 17 true isolates have no edges to be pulled anywhere
by that layout, so they're placed deliberately on an outer ring instead of piling up at the
origin.

```{python}
#| label: fig-network
#| fig-cap: "The Marvel wiki-link network: giant component (red, sized by degree), the Strikeforce: Morituri island (blue), and the 17 isolates (gray ring)."

non_isolate_nodes = [nd for nd in G_und.nodes() if G_und.degree(nd) > 0]
H = G_und.subgraph(non_isolate_nodes)
pos = nx.spring_layout(H, seed=42, k=0.2)

main_extent = max(abs(coord) for xy in pos.values() for coord in xy)
ring_radius = main_extent * 1.6
for i, node_id in enumerate(sorted(isolates)):
    angle = 2 * math.pi * i / len(isolates)
    pos[node_id] = (ring_radius * math.cos(angle), ring_radius * math.sin(angle))

def color_for(node_id):
    if node_id in giant:
        return "#c8102e"
    elif node_id in island:
        return "#1f77b4"
    return "#b0b0b0"

node_colors = [color_for(nd) for nd in G_und.nodes()]
node_sizes = [30 + 6 * G_und.degree(nd) for nd in G_und.nodes()]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 11))
nx.draw_networkx_edges(H, pos, alpha=0.15, edge_color="gray", ax=ax)
nx.draw_networkx_nodes(G_und, pos, node_color=node_colors, node_size=node_sizes, linewidths=0, ax=ax)

top_hub_ids = [nid for nid, _ in sorted(G.degree(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:5]]
label_box = dict(facecolor="white", alpha=0.8, edgecolor="none", pad=1.5)

for i, nid in enumerate(top_hub_ids):
    x, y = pos[nid]
    ax.annotate(name_lookup[nid], (x, y), fontsize=8, ha="left",
                xytext=(main_extent * 1.05, main_extent * 0.9 - i * main_extent * 0.12),
                textcoords="data", bbox=label_box,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="gray", lw=0.6))

island_offsets = [(0, 0.1), (0.15, 0.05), (0.16, -0.05), (0, -0.1),
                   (-0.15, -0.05), (-0.16, 0.05), (0, 0.17), (0.2, 0), (-0.2, 0)]
for (dx, dy), nid in zip(island_offsets, sorted(island, key=lambda x: pos[x][0])):
    x, y = pos[nid]
    ha = "left" if dx > 0 else ("right" if dx < 0 else "center")
    ax.annotate(name_lookup[nid], (x, y), fontsize=7, ha=ha,
                xytext=(x + dx, y + dy), textcoords="data", bbox=label_box)

ax.set_xlim(-ring_radius * 1.15, ring_radius * 1.6)
ax.set_ylim(-ring_radius * 1.15, ring_radius * 1.15)
ax.set_title("Giant component (red) · the 9-character island (blue) · 17 isolates (gray ring)")
ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## What surprised us

Two things stood out once we actually looked, rather than assumed:

1. **The 9-node island isn't noise — it's a whole forgotten team.** Every member —
   Vyking, Radian, Snapdragon, Scatterbrain, Shear, Blackthorn, Toxyn, Backhand, Scaredycat — is
   a member of *Strikeforce: Morituri*, a 1980s spin-off series. They link to each other freely
   but never got cross-linked into the mainstream Marvel universe pages that dominate the giant
   component. A network built purely from wiki-links doesn't know "these are all still Marvel
   characters" — it only knows what editors actually wrote, and apparently nobody writing about
   Spider-Man or the Avengers ever mentioned this team.
2. **The in/out asymmetry is much sharper than the average degree suggests.** The average degree
   is a modest 9.5, but the *range* is wildly lopsided: a max in-degree of 106 against a max
   out-degree of only 28. The average hides just how differently "famous" and "chatty" characters
   behave in this graph.

## Bonus appendix: does the real in-degree look more like an exponential or a power law?

Not required this week, but it came for free from earlier prep work, so here it is. 10,000 draws
each from a synthetic exponential and a synthetic power law (Zipf), compared against the real
(binned) in-degree distribution across all four linear/log combinations.

```{python}
#| label: fig-synthetic-compare
#| fig-cap: "Real in-degree (binned) vs. 10,000-sample synthetic exponential and power-law distributions, all four axis combinations."

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

exp_samples = np.floor(rng.exponential(scale=5, size=10000)).astype(int) + 1
pow_samples = rng.zipf(a=2.0, size=10000)

def raw_distribution_from_samples(samples):
    counts = {}
    for v in samples:
        counts[int(v)] = counts.get(int(v), 0) + 1
    return dict(sorted(counts.items()))

exp_dist = raw_distribution_from_samples(exp_samples)
pow_dist = raw_distribution_from_samples(pow_samples)

exp_prob = {v: c / len(exp_samples) for v, c in exp_dist.items()}
pow_prob = {v: c / len(pow_samples) for v, c in pow_dist.items()}
in_bin_prob_y = [y / len(in_degrees) for y in in_bin_y]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 9))
configs = [
    (False, False, "linear-linear"),
    (False, True, "linear-log"),
    (True, False, "log-linear"),
    (True, True, "log-log"),
]

for ax, (xlog, ylog, title) in zip(axes.flat, configs):
    ax.scatter(list(exp_prob.keys()), list(exp_prob.values()), s=12, color="darkorange", label="exponential")
    ax.scatter(list(pow_prob.keys()), list(pow_prob.values()), s=12, color="teal", label="power law")
    ax.plot(in_bin_x, in_bin_prob_y, "o-", color="crimson", markersize=4, label="real in-degree (binned)")
    if xlog:
        ax.set_xscale("log")
    else:
        ax.set_xlim(0, 60)
    if ylog:
        ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("value")
    ax.set_ylabel("probability")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

On log-log axes, the exponential specimen visibly curves and drops off, while the power law
stays close to a straight line across its whole range — and the real in-degree's binned curve
tracks that straight-line behavior more closely than the curving exponential, especially past
$k+1 \approx 10$. Confidence should stay moderate, though: the real curve is only 7-8 binned
points spanning about two decades, built from a single 303-node sample.
:::
